references.text: Do not oppress a foreigner or mistreat them, for you were foreigners in Egypt. This verse gives the same reason for treating foreigners well.
Do not oppress a foreigner. You know what it feels like to be a stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt.
You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Leviticus 19:34 extends this command to also include foreigners.
The Lord loves the foreigner and gives them food and clothing. You too must love the foreigner, for you were foreigners in Egypt.
Do not detest Egyptians, for you were a stranger in their land. A reminder of Israel's stay in Egypt as the basis for how to treat others.
The second commandment is this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Jesus quotes Leviticus 19:18, which parallels verse 34.
Paul summarizes the law with the command to love one's neighbor as oneself, reflecting the principle in Leviticus 19:34.
The entire law is fulfilled in this one command: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. This builds on the same principle.
The royal law according to Scripture: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. James refers to the same command found in Leviticus 19.
Do not forget hospitality, for by it some have entertained angels without knowing it. An encouragement to welcome strangers.
